title: Thesis Defense: Systems to Automate Data-to-Insight Pipelines
description: Thesis Defense: Systems to Automate Data-to-Insight Pipelines Abstract:Data-driven decision-making is central to modern science and industry, yet transforming raw, heterogeneous data into reliable insights remains difficult to automate. A data-to-insight pipeline must discover relevant data, transform and integrate it, select appropriate analyses, and produce results that users can interpret and act upon. These stages are tightly coupled, and optimizing only for the accuracy of the final output can lead to incoherent, uninterpretable, or poorly grounded pipelines. This thesis develops principles and systems for automating data-to-insight pipelines while making their quality requirements explicit. We argue that reliable automation must account for dependencies between pipeline decisions, expose trade-offs between competing objectives such as utility and interpretability, and evaluate not only the final answer but also the process that produces it. Together, these ideas support automation that preserves both answer quality and pipeline quality. Finally, we examine how recent advances in large language models change the design space for data systems. More flexible models can broaden candidate generation and adaptation, but they do not remove the need for execution, semantic checks, and grounding in the underlying data. The thesis therefore points toward data-to-insight systems that are increasingly autonomous while remaining coherent, interpretable, and verifiable. title: Thesis Defense: Discovering and Removing Latent Failure Modes in Neural Networks
description: Thesis Defense: Discovering and Removing Latent Failure Modes in Neural Networks Abstract: This thesis explores a particular class of neural network failure modes we call latent failure modes. Such failure modes are characterized by being hard to discover for the first time, but easy to reproduce once discovered. Examples of latent failure modes include adversarial examples for image models, jailbreaks and prompt injections for large language models (LLMs), and undesired backdoor behaviors purposefully inserted into the weights of models.     Our exploration of latent failure modes is based on a series of 5 case studies spanning the domains of game-playing, language modeling, and vision. Through these case studies we develop a number of important insights about latent failure modes, including that (a) even very capable AI systems can harbor serious naturally-ocurring latent failure modes; (b) across multiple domains, a promising strategy for finding latent failure modes is to train other AI systems to help find them; (c) a lack of high-quality, easy-to-use benchmarks is holding back progress in discovering and defending against latent failure modes in LLMs; and (d) the version of adversarial robustness most relevant to real-world systems (and the general problem of latent failure modes) is unrestricted adversarial robustness, which, despite receiving relatively little attention, may be more tractable than previously thought.      Taken together, our case studies advance the following conclusion: Although latent failure modes are a pervasive feature of modern AI systems that have resisted a decade of research into removing them, several neglected approaches to discovering and removing them could, with greater investment, substantially improve our ability to build reliable AI systems.  TBD October 27, 2026 CSAIL Forum Jacob Andreas CSAIL MIT Part Of CSAIL Forum 12:00 P - 1:00 P Location TBD
